title: Reverse Linked List
description:
Reverse Linked List

Given the head of a singly linked list, reverse the list, and return the reversed list.

Examples:

  • Input: head = [1,2,3,4,5]
    Output: [5,4,3,2,1]
  • Input: head = [1,2]
    Output: [2,1]
  • Input: head = []
    Output: []

Constraints:

  • The number of nodes in the list is the range [0, 5000].
  • -5000 <= Node.val <= 5000

Follow up: A linked list can be reversed either iteratively or recursively. Could you implement both?

solution_text:
Reverse Linked List

The idea: Right now every node points to the node after it. To reverse the list we simply flip each of those arrows so it points to the node before it. We walk through the list once and re-point one link at a time.

Algorithm (three pointers):

  1. Start with prev = None (there is nothing before the first node yet) and curr = head.
  2. Before we break the current link, remember the next node: next_temp = curr.next.
  3. Flip the arrow: curr.next = prev.
  4. Slide both pointers forward: prev = curr, then curr = next_temp.
  5. When curr becomes None we have walked off the end, and prev is now the new head, so return it.

Why it works (invariant): After processing each node, everything from the original head up to prev is already reversed, and curr is the first node of the not-yet-reversed part. Saving next_temp first is essential — once we overwrite curr.next we would otherwise lose the rest of the list.

Complexity: Time O(n) where n is the number of nodes (one pass). Space O(1) — we only reuse three pointers, no extra list.

Edge cases: An empty list (head = None) returns None, and a single node returns itself — both handled naturally because the loop simply does zero or one iteration.
solution_code:
def reverseLinkedList(head):
    prev = None
    curr = head
    
    while curr:
        next_temp = curr.next
        curr.next = prev
        prev = curr
        curr = next_temp
    
    return prev
